blocks.x: I want to get everybody's name. Can you tell me your right name?
Percy J. Gabriel. The J stands for Julian after my mother.
Do you want me to get my name? Not yet. I want to get a level on him. Okay, and what's today's date?
Let's see, we should put where we're at.
We're on reel number two?

Yeah, we're on reel number two and we're at the Howard Tilton Library and in it is the Latin American Library and we're in the seminar room. And what is the continuation of the Percy Gabriel interview? The 10th of July, 1987.
Yeah, okay. So I think we left off, you were in New York with Bobby Robinson. Yes.

They were talking about you and the pay. Yes, that's when I left and went to Florida. But some of the interesting things that I run into before that, which was, I went to work with Lee Collins. I don't know how he found out about me. Somebody told him about me when I was in New Orleans. I was working at the Moulin Rouge then.
Okay, now that was in the French Quarter.
Yes, that was about 1941.
Could you tell me where Moulin Rouge was?
On Burgundy and Bienville Street. That was owned by Elmo Badon. Elmo Badon, that's Pete Herman's brother-in-law.
Oh, okay.

Pete Herman was my sister and they were clubs were one block apart. So Lee Collins heard about me and sent for me to go to work with them in LaSalle, Illinois, as a teeniest silver Congo. We followed Ethel Waters in there. Now, the funny thing about that, we worked in LaSalle, but we had to live three cities away. Spring Valley we lived in. There was a town in between they called Piru, Illinois. There were no blacks living in those Piru, no LaSalle. And in Spring Valley, there was a total of 23 blacks living in there. And that included the three of us with Lee Collins and I brought a piano player with me. I hope his name would come to me. Walt.
This is Real number 3 and we're still with Percy Gabriel on July 10th, 1987. We were talking about fish fries.
Oh yes.
And you were going to...
Fish fries is something like what people call the house rent parties. Mm-hmm.
We're on Real?
Well you just got the names of all the family.
Yeah, Real 4. This is Real Number 4 with Percy Gabriel and it's still July 10, 1987.
Yeah, it seems that way.

It seems that way. You seem to have done a lot of road work, you're on the road a lot. I always want to ask people what's the best thing about being on the road and what's the worst thing about traveling and being on the road?

Well the hardest thing is getting your proper sleep which you never get. And most of the time was traveling by bus. And accommodations out on the road back then was bad. Because there were not many hotels up until in the 50s where blacks could stay. But another thing about it, according to what band you was with out there, according to what price you paid in hotels. Now that sounds funny. And also in restaurants. Which I was lucky enough, I had sense enough, not to go in a group for meals or to get a place to stay. And I didn't stay in too many hotels.
Where was you staying?

I'd always let the band go where they're going. Then I'd go around, hit some of the bars. Look like, see a fella look like he's in the know. Then I'd go up and ask him, where do he eat? He'd say, oh right down there they got the chicken shack or so and so's resting. But I'd say, now where do you eat? Well I eat around there by Miss So and So. You go around there by Miss So and So's little place, you get a better meal and cost you less money. And then while in there I'll say, well, you know anybody that got a room, you know, they want to rent me out for the night or two. Oh Miss Sarah got a spare room over there. Bessie got a spare room over there. I say, good I'll go over there and don't cost me neither the amount of money that the other fella. I remember one trip was down in Fort Wayne, Indiana. I was playing with Deacon Jones Band out of Toledo. I'll say his band, but I'm the fella who got the band together for him. And the fellas went on and rushed to stay at the motel and the hotel. It was costing them something like $90 a week. And I went across the track to a little hotel and I was paying $10 a week. They was paying $4 or $5 a day per meal. And I was eating at Miss Tubbs restaurant for $8 a week.
That's a good deal obviously.

That's it. Another lady out there in New Iberia, we used to call her Big Sis. When we'd play all through Highway 9, we'd stay in New Iberia. She used to charge us $0.50 a night for rooms. And $0.25 a meal. So I, well, I was quite conservative because I had a family. And I always had to save money to send home. Where most of these fellas out there, they didn't bother with sending any money home. Whether they had a family or not. For instance, they got it. They spent, they looked to borrow for me most of the time. And that happened also when I was working with Jane Mack Shands Band. Fellas couldn't keep a thin quarter in their pocket. Never have over two shirts to wear and do any on one side. Then turn it on the wrong side and wear it again.
Well, was that a problem when you're on the road and you're working, traveling so much? Was that a problem having clean clothes?

Yes, because it's hard. If you didn't have a lot of clothes, it would be hard for you. Like me, I always had like about 30 or 40 shirts. And had change of, I kept a lot of clothes with me on the road. I'd see some of those fellas would travel with a paper bag.
That's no joke.
And I knew how to wash in iron.
Oh, okay.

See, and I'd wash my shirts myself. My underwear, I always washed underwear and socks. I always had a place where I could make sure I could clean myself and clean my clothes. And if I got to somebody's house, I'd borrow an iron. Or sometime I'd find somebody asking if they wanted to do up my shirts. I'd need them for the night. Because I'm leaving them in the morning and they're getting ready. Even now, I mean, that I'm not on the road. Oh, every two or three years when I look down in my closet, I'd give away 15 or 20 shirts. I remember I came down here with about 25 or 30 shirts to give to my brother-in-law. And I have so many shirts now, I don't know what to do. Because my kids are always buying me things. They got to the point now and I said, Daddy, we don't know what to buy you. You got everything. You got so many shirts.
You mentioned Jay McShann's band. Was Charlie Parker in the band when you were in the band?

Charlie Parker rejoined the band while we was working at the Down Beat in New York. That was in 44, 45. And Mike Shan left him right there. Well, no, we didn't leave him in New York. He had to get out of town. Dave Dexter was a talent scout with Capitol Recording Company. The police was looking for Charlie then to put him in jail for dope. And they put him on a train and sent him on out to California. But he worked with us at the Down Beat in New York for about three weeks. That was during the time we had one of the greatest jam sessions I've ever been on. With Charlie? Well, he was in on that session too. It was Duke Ellington, Dorothy Donegan, Art Tatum, and Jay McShann, Coleman Hawkins. Charlie Parker was playing alto. And Paul Quinichet on tenor. That session happened to be held in the Down Beat. We was playing that again. And you were playing?
I was playing bass.
That's hot cock. I mean, that's all those people.
Who's on first now? Who's on first?
No, who played drums? Do you remember? Well, don't worry.
Yeah. Jesse Price was on drums. Oh, really?
Yes. Jesse Price was on drums then.
Oh, really? Yes. Jesse Price was on drums then.
Well, bringing up Charlie Parker, I mean, maybe you can give us your short speech on drugs and music. How prevalent was it when you were coming up?

Drugs was the thing then. I wasn't around Charlie Parker too much to see. Well, I mean, he was stupefied, you know, and I kept my distance from him because if it wasn't something that you could buy legal, I didn't want to be around it. One fellow we had in the band, he was a terrific musician, Lamont Hamilton, tenor player. He was a great musician. We was playing one time at the track as we call it, it's a boy ball room. Lamont played the first one of two nights and he got in with some women there and he'd come to work with his horn at night, come up on the stand, tune his horn up, get out his music, and go sit in the band. And then when we got through playing singing, man, we sure blew, he hadn't blown off the whole night. He did that for three weeks. So I felt bad about it because I am the one who got him in the band because we needed a ton of man when we was in Cincinnati. And I went around the cotton club and Cyril August from here, he was playing alto, Kandy Johnson, tenor, Lamont Hamilton tenor, and the baritone player, he later went with Duke. His name will come to me later, but I told him I said I talked with Kandy, he says, man, no, I said we need a ton of player. It was with Tiny Brideshow, he had a group there. It was one trumpet, trombone, and four reeds in a rhythm section. Tiny was playing piano. So both of them said they would come with the band when we got ready to leave, neither one of them showed up. We happened to meet Lamont in Jacksonville, Florida, and the railroad station stranded there with a band. They didn't know during the war, they didn't know how to travel. If it wasn't essential, they wouldn't let you on the train. But I had a habit, Mike Shea and I would take a $20 bill and put it in our hand, and walk to the man at the gate, the conductor, whichever it was, and shake hands with him with the $20 bill. He said, look, we got to get on this train. He says, well, you walk all the way down to the end, take the band, you go down that track, there ain't no train there. But after you get so far down, then you cross back over where the train was.
That's how we used to get on.

And they didn't know how to do that. So when Lamont saw, he said, man, if you'll get out, I want to go with the band. He said, I'm sorry, I didn't meet so. Look, yeah, I talked to Mike Sand, Mike Sand took him. That's why I felt responsible for him. Then, I didn't know he was an Army deserter.
Oh, God.

I was hooked up all kinds of ways and didn't know. I found that out, we were playing a lot of Army camps and naval bases. And he was right there with us, not saying anything. So we played three states in one day. We left from Milwaukee, Wisconsin, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Sioux City, Iowa, and Great Bench, Kansas. That night we ended up. And we played there and here was the FBI in there. Called me over, two young fellas, you know. And they called about four or five names of Lamont that I didn't know. They were checking me out first. And I said, yeah, you're trying to play Lamont. I said, what do you mean? He's on me. I said, no, I said, man, he's been with us. I said, yeah, we know. And they started calling everywhere we had been. He says, now you're the one who got him in the band, so we're going to let it up to you to get him to turn himself in. I said, because if we take him in there, there's something to shoot him as a deserter during war. I talked with him. He said, well, look, man, we're headed to Toledo, Ohio. He said, I want to see my dad before I go in. He said, when we get to Toledo, I'll go out to Detroit. That's only 60 miles away. I said, my dad, he turned myself in. I said, look, man, I'm going to keep close eye on him because I don't want that people. They're holding me responsible for you. So he did. But to see Drugs do a person like that, that he didn't know nothing. He thought he was playing the whole night. He was sitting in a booth with a woman. And Mike Shan wanted to leave in New York. I said, no, my, we took him out. I think Don Byers played, but we was playing along with Erskine Hawkins and Tab Smith during that time.

You brought up a point about, you've worked with a lot of big band leaders. Oh, yeah. Jay McShann. How do you, how do you rate Jay McShann? How was Jay McShann as a band leader as opposed to maybe other people?

To me, Jay McShann was terrific. And he's a terrific pianist. A lot of people here play in the blues, but they don't know that McShann is a concert pianist. Also a great organist, which he played around Kansas City years back. And he's not, people think he's from Kansas City, he's not. He's from Oklahoma. Think it's Oklahoma, Oklahoma. That's his home. He came into Kansas City. But he is a terrific musician. And maybe I liked him because he had so much interest in me, you know what I mean? He said I'm the only one who had a level. He didn't use no dope. And most of the time he would give me money. If he wasn't gonna leave with the band right then, he'd give me money to charter a bus. Or get a train and take the rest of the band on.
You mean the whole band was using dope?
No, no.

Just about. Just about. Well, no, there was a baritone player from out of Chicago. He didn't use any dope. He was regular with the band. Most of them was using, you know, like grass, marijuana, which wasn't too bad then. But the only one that I knew went off was at Lamont. What he was using, he had to be using cocaine or morphine something when he hit New York. And even I've seen him recently, just before I left Detroit, he's back around there. And he's got an old woman that keeps it pretty straight. He's not going off too much. He may use a little grass, but I don't think he's going into any type of cocaine or morphine or anything like that. But just about all the other fellas in the band use something. And I never do see Mike Shan use anything but gin. Him and I used to keep us a fifth or two of gin together. Right.
So that's your only vice. Yeah.
If he used anything, he didn't let me see him do it.
Maybe, Dick, we talk about recordings because you played with so many different bands. Did you ever record with Jamie Shan? Yes, I recorded with Mike Shan, yeah.
Yeah, I did about... What tracks, I mean, what songs you did?
Twelve recordings.

I recorded with Mercury. And, oh, I can, with Jimmy Witherspoon singing. Charles Waterford singing. We did a lot of recording in St. Louis. We did some recording in California. Mm-hmm. Now, I don't keep them. Only a couple of the numbers. One I can remember because I named the number and it was my idea. It was a number we called Bucktown Boogie. I thought about this little place we used to come. My daddy used to play out in Bucktown. Mm-hmm. And, I was featured solo on it. I had one record and I loaned it to a musician live across the street from me and I haven't seen it since.
Yeah.
But I did a lot of recording around here. Oh, with Roy Brown one night. I think...
I was going to ask you about Roy Brown. Yes.
I think I did about, oh, 20 some sides with Roy Brown. I recorded with Danny and Lou Barker on Capitol. I recorded with a singing group in Chicago. I can't even remember the group.
Mm-hmm. Did you enjoy making records? Was that...

Oh, yes. We used to have fun back then because I remember we recorded on Deluxe Records here, but we used to get a couple of bottles, you know, and we had more like fun, laugh and talk and just have drinks. We went in the studio one night.
Was that here?
Here, yes, on the main in Claiborne, or the main in Ramport Street I think it was.
J and L.
Went in there recording say like about five, six o'clock in the evening. And we didn't finish recording until about four or five o'clock the next morning.
How did you get anything to eat? Oh, they went out and got us sandwiches.
And it was, we recorded like say about 20 or 30 sides. Yeah. Like I tell you, we was having a party with, you know, we had drinks and sandwiches in there.
These were records for Roy Brown.
Yes. The Roy Brown stuff.
Do you remember who was on those tracks for Roy Brown?

Walter Daniels, Edgar Blanchett was on them too. Now if I got a footnote, one of my footnotes, I could tell you everybody on there because they knew and I didn't know. I was on the cover footnotes from out of England.
Yeah. We saw that.

And they got all the recordings I made. I made a lot of recordings with Danny that I forgot about until I went, looked through there, the recordings. Yeah, they had them. And then I remember, oh yes, I did do this or I did that, you know.
Could you tell me about the recording process at that time? Except for at Cosmos, at J&M.

Well let's say we were getting $42 a session then. And it was only allowed to make full sides, a limit of two hours. But they didn't have so much frills in these recordings. You may have an echo chamber and that's about all. And you went in there, you run down what you were going to do. You remember saying you had a sound, good, go ahead, let's cut it. It was very seldom you had to make remakes on it, retakes. But nowadays recording is, oh you're sitting up there with some earphones on you, you in one room and makes instruments in the other room. We was all in one big room and everybody had a mic in the front of you, went on and did it. I did some recording recently and I will not use, let the fellas use earphones. I want them all close together so we know what we're doing.
Well thank God somebody's got some sense.
I wanted to follow up, were you a member of Roy Brown's band? Did you tour with him?
No, I played a couple of times with him but I wasn't a member of his band. You just made the record dates. Yeah, that was just a little bunch of wild kids, you know.
Well that was a question I was going to get to. They called that music that Roy Brown was doing at that time, rhythm and blues music. Yes. Did you take it seriously? Did jazz musicians?
Yeah, I take it seriously. Anything I do I take it seriously.
But you said they were a bunch of wild kids.

Yes, but I mean they just asked me to come out and record. And I think it was Paul Gaten had me to come out on this session. But these kids, you know some of those kids he had playing with them, but Roy didn't even know what key that was playing in.
I'm not kidding. So there was something substandard?

He wanted good piano player. Walter Daniels was a good piano player. Edgar Blanchett was a good guitar player. So he got us together to make the records. But one of those saxophone players used to call him Wild Man. The band sounded good, you know, for what he was doing when he got out there on the road. But most of those kids they didn't know what they were doing.
You reminded me, did you know a guy named Batman?
Batman was in there, yeah, Batman was the title. Well that's what we called him, Wild Batman. He was a tenor player in the band.
Yeah, his name was Leroy Rankins?
Yes, I think he's dead.
Yeah, yeah, it was Batman.
Just about all those youngsters in that group are dead. Was there Cat Man too?
Cat Man was another, there was another tenor man.
Yeah, I don't know him.
There was a Cat Man. Cat Man? Yeah, Robert Catman. That was Cat Man.
Yeah, he and there was, little Al was out with him playing bass. Al? Yeah.
Brown skin fella? Yeah, little thin fella.
I think he died too.
I don't know who that is.

Yeah, Al died in, oh, Gishaw and I don't know. I think I don't know. I think I don't know. Yeah, Al died in, oh, Gishaw and I don't know. Gishaw and he died, all those fellas. I mean, they didn't take care of their self out there on the road. Wow.
Dick, did you have anything, I wanted to ask him some things about nightclubs, some different nightclubs. Well, let's go through the records. Oh, okay. I've got some things I just want to ask.
The piano player with Danny Barker, Joe, did you know his last name? Joe? You gave it two different names for the guy in books.
That we record here?
Yeah, and you know, with Louise and Danny.
Let's see, now I'm trying to think who was on. I think Walter Daniels recorded with us too.
Yeah. He could have. They had Joe Pears or Joe Parrish.

Joe Parrish. They called him Joe Parrish. We called him Joe Parrish. He's in Chicago now. Yeah. He's a terrific pianist, terrific vibe man too. Yeah. I just talked with him three weeks ago. I was coming from Minnesota and I stopped in Chicago.
Do you know how to spell his last name? I think it was P-I-R-S, Paris. Well, we can check with the local. Yeah.

And his wife is here. Oh. Yeah, I think his wife is here. He told me she's still staying here in New Orleans. Because he left her here years ago. We did some recording. We did a couple of sessions and Joe's got on one number on that. I was featured on it during Willow Weep for Me. And the other side of it, we call it Mop Mop Brown. It was the changes to Sweet Georgia Brown. And we used those changes, but our whole melody and call it Mop Mop Brown. It's Joe Parrish by South On Bass. And I think Freddie Coleman's on drums. The tenor player with Fats Domino, Tall Collies. Where's his name start with L, is it? Lionel or Leon something?
Oh, it'll come to me. Yeah, I think he's still with Fats. Yeah, he probably is. Yes.
Four, five pieces. Curtis Trevino was playing guitar. Curtis Trevino, guitar.
Isn't that somebody named Kimble that plays tenor with Fats?
Kimble. With Fats? Kimble played bass. Now this is another one.
It's a Kimble, yeah. Young guy. Kimble, what's Kimble's name? No, don't worry. Yeah, who plays with Fats now.
Well, I've been away from here so long, you know, just kidding. I don't keep up with the younger fellas.
Where were you when you, well, did you record with Walter Brown?

No, Walter Brown had already made his hits, Confessing the Blues and so forth. Yeah. And Walter Brown, well, let's say, did we have, I don't remember whether we had a session with Walter Brown or not. But anyway, the only one thing I could remember about Walter Brown, we played the Paradise Theatre in Detroit. Mm-hmm. And Walter Brown run up a big bill at the hotel, Gotham Hotel. And he wanted Mike Shan to pay the bill, it was more than his salary. And it seemed like Walter Brown must have had a habit of doing those things. And Mike Shan wouldn't do it, and Johnny Tamina wouldn't do it. So he'd say, if you all owe pay the bill, I'm not going to pay you, and I'm going to leave the band. So, Mike Shan said, that's your business. So we took off without him, we'd pick up Scott Man Bailey. Oh, yeah. And when we got here, we did a recording session here. I had the band, and I used Earl Palmer on drums. My brother, man, he was on clarinet. Well, he was on trumpet. He was in Lyra's band, too, and he's quit playing, so I understand Danny tried to get him back. And Walter Daniels was on piano on that. Joe Phillips on trumpet. Yeah. I don't know, we got paid for the session. We did it somewhere on Canal Street in a block or two from Whirline's. And I don't know what became of those records after that. I didn't hear any more. That's Scott Man Bailey?
Yes. Is he any kid to Blues Bailey? That was Blues Bailey.

Oh, that's the same guy. We called him Blues Scott Short Light Skin Fella. Yeah, that's the same one. He worked with Mike Shanawal, and he stayed here. And we worked on Canal Street with Joe Paz on piano at a supper club. And hardly anybody come in, but this was for another gangster here. So I understand he was supposed to be serving 99 years in a pen that was doing. Earl Long was governor then. And he was in his club every night.
Yeah. You mentioned Joe Paris. Was that Joe Paris who also played Vibes? Yes. And he also played Vibes. Yeah, that's him. You know how to spell his name? I think it's P-A-I-R-S.

Yes, P-A-I-R-S, that's it. Yeah, well, we did. But it's no trouble. I can get, I can get his, I don't have his telephone number with me, but it's no trouble. All I got to do is call Pearl, Judge Rowley's wife. He was a drummer and a bass player too. Yeah, Judge Rowley. Yeah, we were good friends in Chicago. And he was a drummer.
Now who was Jim Taylor?

Jim Taylor, he was a jazz promoter. He had the Hot Jazz Society. And he's not into any of that anymore. And he was into recording. And he tried to bring back the McKinney Cotton Pickers, called it Little McKinney, New McKinney Cotton Pickers. But it was, actually it was only two men he started with that played with the McKinney Cotton Pickers. That was the guitar player, the banjo player that died and was doing the singing.
Was that before Dave Wilber or after?

That was Dave Wilber and that was when he started it. Oh, that's right. And one of the saxophone players, which he died and all the rest was white in the band. And they got some of those old Don Redmond arrangements. And they were going pretty good for a while. And then the bottom dropped out.
Yeah.
Now the fellow plays trumpet with me, Charles Victor Moore, he's one of the Cotton Pickers. Mm-hmm. And he wasn't even in the band.
Yeah.

See, they used to advertise as the only living Cotton Pickers, which there was about three fellows still living. Yeah. And then somehow another, the band and Jim Taylor got into it. After Jim Taylor got a whipping, the band just dropped out. Now they got one or two fellows every year when the Montreux is there, they get up to slow five or six pieces and see the new McKinney Cotton Pickers and play one or two jobs with them. And then the fellows are scattered around. Tom Saunders was in that band. And the fellow who had the band short, he left and he went to California. And I can't hear, I've worked with him on a couple of jobs under his name of some of the ski lodges. But that's the other many cotton, McKinney Cotton Pickers was the tempo was too fast and they started at a hotel there. And I had to laugh in Detroit. And somebody told me about it and I went and talked with the man. And I figured I'm working right along with them, which they was only working one evening a week there. But I got more money for my six pieces than they got for those whole 12 pieces. And when they found out the money, I was getting, they got mad and worked that one evening a week that they were working. And then the world's greatest jazz band came in with Hank.

Is this on? Are we gone? Okay. Recording things on, the lights on, so I guess we're rolling. Okay, this is what, we're on reel number five with Percy Gabriel and we're, it's reel number five. And July the 10th, 1987, so we're continuing. I had some questions about nightclubs in New Orleans and different...
Let's see. What reel is this? This must be the six, huh? Yeah, number six. Percy J. Gabriel Sr. the 10th of July 1987 and Tad Jones has left. I was gonna ask you, did you record with Perch?
No, I don't think I've recorded with Perch.
Yeah, okay.

He worked with me also here at the Molen Rouge. I had him with me at one time. Oh, really? I had Manuel Krustow playing trumpet with me at one time. With Jack Lamont on clarinet. I had Hilde on trumpet with me at one time. As a matter of fact, I kept a good group of- Toots played piano with me after my brother went in service. Little Daddy played piano with me for a while there.
What was Little Daddy's brother's name? Which Little Daddy is this?
Little Daddy piano player, a little short fella. Last time I saw him, he was pretty sick. He could hardly walk. If I heard his name, I would know him.
Was he, did he, did you know Kid Ernest?
Kid Ernest, yes.
Moliere was his name?
Yeah, yeah, I think that was Daddy's name, last name Moliere.
Yeah, well they were brothers, so they might have the same name. Doesn't always happen. You know, but now you were talking about Kill D. Yes. What kind of trumpet player was he? How did he play?
Kill D was a hell of a trumpet player and a ranger. He was from out of Joe Robichaud's band also. I think he was in Celestan's band at one time.
Oh yeah. So he could get off?
Oh yeah, Kill D was terrific. One of the numbers that Charlie Parker, they claimed to be Charlie Parker and Dipaldi, I'm sure that was Kill D's number.
Yeah. Now, do you know Kill D's name?
I have forgotten. I knew his name.
Yeah, well it doesn't matter, I've got it somewhere. I got him to sign a book I had once. I met him at the J&M studios.
He's been there for quite a while too.
Yeah. Record shop there. Yeah, he has been for a while now. Did they have any other arrangers here in town?

Oh yes, well like that most of the fellas were doing for quite a while. Well, a lot of the arrangements from Offer Records, different bands were making because Ella Fitzgerald was out to see. She was in the band, her and Hot Lips and Pig Lake Bates was in the band when I played with Andy Kirk. Really? Yeah, Ella Fitzgerald and Pig Lake Bates. They were with Kirk? They were traveling with Kirk? That's right, yeah, they was traveling with Kirk.
Well, what-
That's how I got to work with them.
I never saw Bates. What did he do actually?
He was a tap dancer with a leg and a peg. They call it peg leg peat. One legged.
But he could actually tap dance.
He could actually tap dance. Yeah. That's him. He was good.
Yeah. That's incredible.
But you know like, like Billie Holiday, well I knew her from around New York.
Mm-hmm.
This Billie Holiday story, you may have seen the movie of it. No, I heard her though. Well you heard of it. No, I heard her on the record.
Oh you heard of it. That was enough. I don't want to see any of that job.

Well part of that was in the movie where she threw the gin on this promoter. Yeah. Actually that was me she threw the gin on. Oh I see. She wanted to throw it at Buster, her piano player. And I walk in the door at the time, she splashed when I was in Club Nemo in Detroit.
And his name was Buster, huh? Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah, well, but Billie Holiday, I don't see why they rated us so great because I didn't care for so much but because she always sang behind the beat.
Mm-hmm.

And I remember when she was on the show where we were playing, I told Johnny, he was directing the band, and she had her own pianos there. Mm-hmm. And I said, Johnny, keep your tempo. Don't worry about how she's singing, you keep your tempo. So, Johnny went to, she was doing Lover Man, and she slows it down, you know. Mm-hmm. And Johnny went to slow down with her, and she turned around, she said, play the music, goddammit, I'll be at the end with you. Yeah? Yes, I had to let, from that time on I said, now you know what I mean, I told you, keep your tempo, don't slow down with her. Sure. Because she was, when I first knew her, she was working at the YAM Man, one of them little joints in New York. They used to have so many joints around, they'd meet the greatest.
Could she make change? Oh, yes. Oh, yeah. She, she, I mean, in that club. Yeah.
But you see, uh.
I mean, like put 50 cents on the corner of the table?

Well, no, I never saw her do that, but Hazel Ballot, and quite a few others, they'd do it, you know. Yeah. I seen them put a stack of diamonds. Yeah. And they'd pick up a stack of diamonds, they'd pick up a paper dollar off the table. Yeah.
Well, I guess they, they were well educated.
Oh, yeah. They'd dance up to it, and. Yeah. Snatch it back.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, I've seen quite a few of them. I never saw any of these women around New Orleans do that, but around New York, Chicago, they could do it. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But, uh. We used to have some sessions, as I started to tell you about that, that's how I run into Stuff Smith, they used to be in there jamming, Eddie South, Shramea Young. Where was this? At the Big Apple in New York. Yeah. They used to come in there around one, two o'clock in the morning. Sometimes we'd have as much as 15, 20 pieces in there. That's what actually ruined music around New York quite a bit. Uh-huh. Back then, thirties and forties, man would hire a piano and drum. Cause he knew so many musicians was gonna come in and sit in, they wouldn't hire anymore. Yeah. And, uh, Harry James and all those fellas used to come up there. They'd have four or five white, maybe about four or five white, everybody in there jamming
together. Yeah.

That's one thing, uh, with the music, between the musicians there, there's no color. Uh-huh. We was on tour, I remember, with a trombone player, formerly of, who was with, uh, Louis Armstrong, uh, for a while. T. Gordon.
Uh-huh.

And we played quite a few places together. And, funny thing, we, they had to pay, when we were playing these different army camps, we'd go into officers' quarters and eat, and they made tea garden and he's bad paying.
Oh, no.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah, we, we could, we could have been arrested when we were, uh, playing at that place on bourbon, at 1111 bourbon, I don't know, with Danny and Louise and, uh, and, uh, Albert Walters. Well, here they didn't bother you.
Yeah. Because when I worked at the Mullen Ruards, uh, I played and emceed the show for white striptease acts.
Uh-huh.
And I don't mean come down to the G-string, they came down to their birthday club.
Yeah.
And I remember one time, Miss Wurrlein tried to get them to pass a law that every nightclub had a show and had a black band that had to have a screen in front of the band.
Uh-huh.

Some of them did it. When they come to Elmore, Elmore told them I'd be damned if I'm doing it. And she tried for her doing this to get it done. Uh-huh. But they wouldn't do it at our place. The doghouse had it for a while. And, uh, Puffy House and them had shoes there. They had a little place, Searrow. Searrow's in Fernhorn. Biamble between Bourbon and Royal, I think it was. I worked in there for him. And I also was booking bands in there for him. I supplied it one time, I was the only black band out in the French quarters. And, uh, Howard would play sometime, but regular bands, no.
Tiro Calico, was that the guy? I forgot. A little short guy.

Yeah, a little short Italian fella. Gray hair. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And, uh, and everybody saw what a good band we had. And we was there on time every night. And they used to come around to me and ask, can they get a band, could I have a band like me. And I must have put about five or six different bands out there in the French quarters. Yeah. Well, Cole, Tucker Cole, he passed away in Chicago. Now he was stranded here in New Orleans some time ago. And I started him out in the French quarters. I started Laverne Smith out in the French quarters, at Tony Pesina's place. See, Tony Pesina, we come up in the same neighborhood. He was around, his dad had a grocery on Bianville and Miro, and I was at the next corner, the Cornine Miro.
You talking about which Tony Pesina's place?
He used to have a place on, uh, just off of, what did you call it? Just off of Bourbon Street, the gay place he had. Toulouse. Toulouse, yeah.
He used to have a couple places.
Yeah, and he went somewhere else. He had a woman, Johnson, this woman who played a kid. Gracie. Gracie, yeah. They all went, the whole family I think ended up out in California.
Yeah, Plaz is her.
Plaz Johnson, one of our sons. They were doing good out in California the last I heard.
Somehow that reminds me, uh, cause her son recorded with Pernell, Alton Pernell.
Yes. He just recently died.
Yeah. When he was playing in the same band with you, how did he play? What kind of piano play?
He played the same style piano.
Same as Laverne.
Yeah, he played with Rainey's band. I played with him along there.
Yeah.
And Houston, William Houston came into Rene's band after that. And then he was also in Sidney Desvinge's band when I played with him.
Well, did, would Pernell play chords? Did he know a lot of chords then? Was he just learning?
Well, he played chords and played solos. He wasn't, I never look at him as a great piano player or anything, but he made it. Yeah.
Did he have good rhythm?

I, yeah, he was, he was pretty good. Good touch? Yeah, he was. You know, uh, he was with the band. He wasn't with the others in the band too long with him because not long after he come in the band is when I left and went to New York with Harold Dajon. Mm-hmm. That's when we took Blackie San Diego. Yeah. Because, uh, Pernell was playing with Harold a while and Harold got rid of Pernell and took Blackie. Yeah. His brother. Well. They tell me Pernell tore up New York and they went and got R.T. in my thing for him. That's the way they told me.

But anyway, somebody like Pernell, you know, it seems to me that when I heard him, he was playing solo piano, that must have been in the 40s, late 40s. You know, maybe Dan's International or someplace like that. And, uh, he could do that. But I wondered how he was in a band in a rhythm section. Because you never know unless you're in the rhythm section.
Yeah, well.
Is what I'm asking.
Clarence Tisdale was playing banjo in the band too. So, it wasn't, you didn't have to worry too much because Clarence, all he played was rhythm.
Mm-hmm.
And that helped. And Joe Rainey was a hell of a rhythm man too.
Yeah.
So, between Joe Rainey, Clarence and myself, you didn't have to worry much what the piano was doing outside of solos.
How did Joe feel about religion then? Was he talking about religion all the time?
No, he wasn't. No, he wasn't. He played a little clarinet too every night and then. He'd pick up the clarinet and play a little something and be right for something.
Yeah, well you know he later was very religious.
I think he was a Jehovah Witness or something somebody told me.
Yeah, that's when I knew him. But he'd talk about music. He didn't turn his back on the music world or anything. No. He was a very open, honest, and funny sort of guy. He had a good sense of young.
He was a different attitude than his brother. Oh yeah. Kid Rene was more a ladies man. Yeah.
I guess Joe was too fat for that.

Rene, you see Rene was right in our neighborhood. Rene lived on Corn Eyre between Johnson and Gallows I think it was. Did he drink? Yeah, he used to drink but then he on the end of it he had to quit drinking. Because I think when I was working with him he didn't drink anyone. See all of us played with Rene. Yeah. My brother-law August played with him, my brother Clarence played with him, my brother Manny played with him and I played with him.
Well how was he playing when you were with him?

He was playing good. He was terrific then. Because I remember Louis Armstrong, Johnny Tessiturn had Louis Armstrong eat at the Coliseum Arena. And then he came over to the tea room because him and Rene was buddies. And by the way my daddy was the first manager of the Coliseum Arena. Really? But he wouldn't keep it and he said he just told the man, he was a friend of the owner, I don't remember his name. He said I just want to give a dance or two here. I remember the dance he gave there. Louis Armstrong played the advertisement for him that day. And Sidney Desiree played the dance that night. And that was the same, the last job Louis Armstrong played before he went away. He left town the next day and went away. And that was the Chicago. Did Rene have much range when you were playing with him?

Yeah he had, doing good range. Could he make those pedal tones? Yes. Could he get down low? He was in full action of his horn. He was playing every night, seven nights a week. I got an album of Rene at my house. Well do you think that sounded anything like it?

Yes. Those are old thick records. I think it's full sides to the album, two thick records. I was telling the fellow around there, could I earn it for you? Yeah. And he asked me questions about the musicians here and what he found out. And he asked me questions about the musicians here and what he found out. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. and I was trying to think, Matthew played trombone on it. Bill? Bill Matthews was on it.
Oh, really?
Yes.
Well, you know, I never didn't like those records he made very much, because I didn't think it showed what he could do.
He could play, you know, it didn't show his- They were limited on those records. I think he's playing Panama on it.
Yeah.

I don't touch him too much, because one of them has a piece crack out of him. Yeah. And I just keep it more so of remembrance of Rainey, because he liked me, I was a little kid, you know. Well, I only heard him once,
and I was just passing through town. I think I was in the Navy then, or I was-
Well, you see, I'm going back to 37. Yeah. But he was blowing then.
Well, he could blow when I heard him much better than on the records, you know. And he went way up above the staff, and all that stuff, you know.

Well, he was going up there then, because they used to call him then, when I was playing with him, the Louis Armstrong of the South, like he used to say. Sure. Tell Armstrong, you keep it going up the line, and I'd be back here, because they wouldn't say up north, they'd say up the line.
Yeah.
And I got it down here.
Yeah.
We had one of the hottest little bands around here, when I was with Rene.
Oh, sure.

Yeah, he was, you know what I mean, he don't get the credit that he really deserved. They gave more credit to fellas like Thomas Jefferson, than they gave to Rene. But you see, them old fellas and band leaders, they used to pull some deals off. I played with T-Boy Remy. And he took me on a job up to Raceland. I didn't know it was going to be a taxi dance. Yeah. I'm looking for a player that we have intermission. He said, what you want to stop for? I said, man, at least I got to go in the trailer, get a drink. Go ahead and come on by if we keep playing. Mm-hmm. And the job only paid $4. Mm-hmm. So fella picked us up in a truck, you know, and rode us to the ferry, Jackson Street. Mm-hmm. We caught the ferry and come over. He still hadn't paid me.
Mm-hmm.
And we got on a Jackson Street car and we're coming.
He said, man, what about my money?
Oh, yeah, all right. And like he was going to get off at the next corner, and then he gave me my money, rolled up.
Mm-hmm.

When I look at it, it was $3.75 instead of $4. That quarter meant a lot. My man, that's a fella who booked us. I said, man, if I'm a catcher, I'll break your name. Don't call me to book. That's for that quarter. And another time we was on a job, we went, I don't know who was playing, but I think Joe Rene was on that job. Bill Matthews. We went down the valley or a bureau somewhere down the line. Mm-hmm. Off the river. Those people had a big table spread out with food. But me, I'm a young fella with the band. All of them old timers reach and look like they got five arms coming off each body. When they got through reaching, there was one meatball left.
Oh, man.

So the lady, these kids would come there, raise themselves, and we all didn't leave the little kid nothing. I said, that's all right. There's one meatball that they had, what you call, Dove and Spaghetti, chicken meatball. And a big piece of meatball. And a big piece of chunks of meat like that. And she said, that's right. Come here, son. She took me on the side to fill my plate up. She said, now here, you eat, you don't eat with them.
I said, I'm nice waiting instead of me grabbing like them.

No. They grabbing that one meatball left. And I'm surprised. If I wouldn't have reached for that, but I wouldn't have got that one meatball. So I come back. I was telling my brother Clarence about it. He said, look, next time you get out there, you reach. When they reach, you reach with both hands. See, because that's the way they're all. They'll eat up everything you install. Yeah. Yeah. But I learned a lot from those fellas, you know. Old Tom Copen, another bass player. I've been trying to think of him. I remember he was playing for a win on Corn Eye, a girl I went to school with, on Corn Eye between Russian Blade and Tartee. And my brother, man, he yelled, come on, let's go cut his head. Come on, let's go. He used to take me around. Yeah. Everybody hit me, but I got to cut his head, you know. So I learned one thing from him. He used to play some. He played that once, and I got it, and I started doing it more. He said, oh, that kid can play. Let him be letting me sit up and play it almost a whole night. He gave almost a whole night for him. Yeah, but man, he had that. I remember one time they was rehearsing at the Tulane Hall, a WPA band. And he used to try to get me to join a WPA band. I said, no, man, I'm working on nightclubs. I ain't thinking about it. But WPA band, all them fellas, they wasn't working on nightclubs. They got a job maybe once every month or maybe twice a month, one deal like that. Yeah, I'm working regular. So I happened to come up there when we went on it, and Sun Johnson and about three or four of us were just playing together. And I'm on, I forgot whose bass it was. It must have been Albert Glennie. I think he was in his bass or somebody's bass that playing. Boy, that band conductor come in and he heard us there. He jumped all over them. By me being in that playing, which I just said, good day. I turned around, walked around. And he wanted to find out who I was. He invited me to join a dude. I couldn't be, you know what I mean? I couldn't be with music. It's always something happy to me. The main thing while I still stick with it, I'm glad to get out there and make people smile, make people laugh, you know? And when I see an audience, some ignorant person in it, like he come over there, I can't even think of his name, which it don't mean nothing to me. Who was the conductor of the WPA band?
They had several of them. Not Vince Facturo, Louis Dumaine.

That was before Louis Dumaine. Louis Dumaine was the... Martin Martinez. Yeah, yeah, him, Martinez. Joe Martinez. Yeah, he was an evil... The way he used to holler at them fellas, like if there was dogs, I heard him.
This is a white man? Yeah. Yeah, that's Martinis, I guess.
Yes. Louis Dumaine used to... My brother Clarence used to play with Louis Dumaine. They had a band together. Mm-hmm. Yeah, Louis Dumaine, now he was another good trumpet player. Yeah.
His records still stand up from 1927. Yes.

Yeah, I'd sit down every now and then and grab a book and read and see those fellas. I think about when they used to come around the house. Clarence, I think, he played banjo and he played piano with them. See, he did a lot of playing out there at the Diamond Dance joints.
Mm-hmm.
And...
Like which? Do you know them?

The Levita was one of them. Mm-hmm. I think there was one on Iberville between Rapport and Burgundy. Mm-hmm. And there was one on the corner of Burgundy. The Burgundy and Canal are going upstairs. Clarence played there a long time. But I remember the Levita.
Now, where was the Alamo?
The Alamo. That's the Alamo. Okay. It was upstairs on Canal and... either Canal and Burgundy or Canal and Dauphin.
Yeah, well, we can figure it out.

Yes. And there was another one on St. Charles and Canal. I went in that one once, but... Mike DeLay was one of the fellas used to play him, and Albert Fernandes. I remember Albert Fernandes. He would... When Clarence took a break, he'd jump on the piano. Mm-hmm. And... Oh, because Clarence was playing banjo with him too, and he would jump on it. And Mike, he would get on the piano, and Albert would play trumpet. Mm-hmm. And there was one of those brothers, a hell of a musician alto player. There was quite a few brothers. Not the Morgan, but the something else. I used to go around there, and Clarence, when Clarence was playing, I wanted to go out, and all I had to do was walk in there, and he knew I wanted some money. Okay, all right, here it is. Where you going tonight? I'll meet you. Come out of Astoria after you get through, because they used to go by the Astoria and play polka dice there for cigarettes.
Mm-hmm.
And if I had any of my friends would be, he'd treat us, he'd buy us meals and drinks there at Astoria. That used to be the regular hangout there.
Mm-hmm.

And when I came by, I started to see that old group of musicians going out around there, and things had changed so much. Yeah. Oh, Octave used to play in one of the plays with them. Octave was a good chord piano player. Rarely I ever heard him play a solo, and he played with Celestad's band, he played with all those bands, but he was a good rhythm man, but I don't ever remember hearing him play a solo.
Well, maybe that's what made him a good rhythm man. But he played good chords. Yes.
Let me see. Yeah, he knew his chords.
And you said there was a saxophone player that would come in.
Yeah, I'm trying to think of his name. He had some brothers, and I remember he used to take the violin parts and play his part off of them.
He could read them.
Very good reading, transposed right on the spot. Darkfellow, and he played those types of dances quite a bit.
Could, I want to ask you about a saxophone player that you're on me. Could John Handy read?

Most of the time John Handy always had his own band, so I don't know if he read or not. Yeah. He had a brother playing bass, a left-handed fella. He was playing bass before me, and they'd come along and I was trying to help him out there. Yeah. A cap in hand, we called him.
Syl, Sylvester was the brother.
Yes.
Yeah. Gosh, it's so hard to remember all the different ones. I never heard Son Johnson play alto.
Well, Son Johnson was one of the best musicians around. He arranged to.
Mm-hmm.
He was, I mean, one of the best. All of a sudden they tell me he quit and I wouldn't play anymore. He used to like me when I was in a band with them, Herb and Leary.
Mm-hmm.

They had two of us playing, August and myself, you know. Yeah. And he used to like me to be right behind me and say, come on, because you push me when I'm playing. Yeah. Yeah, he was a good son. Tell me he's got a couple of sons that are good musicians.
I only know Ralph, and he plays Reeds too.
And he's played, is he in the Dirty Dozen band? Not that I know of.
He may be now, but I don't know. He's been playing with Placide Adams.
Oh yes, that's my son. Yeah.
Yeah. Oh, when did Clarence, your brother, quit playing?
It must have been, oh he had quit before the 50s. Mm-hmm. And then he went back to playing a little, and then he quit all together. You see, Clarence had a stroke.
Mm-hmm.
I had him in Chicago, and he tore up Chicago.
Really?
Yeah, we was, I was playing with the Lama trio then. We was at the Three Deuces, Wabash and Van Buren.
Mm-hmm.

And I made a trip here, and him and a brother-in-law of mine, Joel of mine, said, well, Joe had a sister in Chicago, and he wanted to come and visit his sister anyway, because there wasn't much work around here. And I told Lee College, my brothers, he said, bring him here. And they wanted him to play solo piano at this place where Lee College was playing. Mm-hmm. And he just sat in, Lee told him that, look at him, I don't want you to hear one of my homeboys. Yeah. And Clarence got on the piano, man hiding right there. I think. In Chicago. In Chicago. I can't think of the name of the place was, but it was somewhere, somewhere on, not far from the Blackstone Hotel.
I don't remember Chicago that way. Yeah. And I don't remember many places. Yeah. Did you ever go to the Victory Club there?
Victory, Victory.
I don't know, that's just one place I can think of. No, I don't think.
Because most of the-
Jeep Robinson used to play there.

Yeah, but most of the time I was in Chicago, I was always working. Yeah. Because we were Jeep, and a woman playing piano, she used to sing with Duke Elminton. I got a picture, I look at her picture the other day. Beverly Thomas, I think. Beverly, Beverly something, her name.
My Pierre?
I can't think of the last name. I'm all looking at. We opened a cabin in the skies from after Walters. At 63rd and Cottage.
Mm-hmm.

And, see, like I tell you, I was all, everywhere I went, I was always working. Oh, shit. Now, like the one time in California, when I quit Mike Shan and Cobb, I worked a little in my cousin owned a cleaning shop at another property, I worked a little in there. And then, Jesse Price, he quit, and we come, we got this group together, and we went right on down to San Diego. Yeah. We worked, oh, we recorded out there, too.
Mm-hmm.
On Capitol. Now, you see, I get to talk like that, and then I get to thinking of some of the people I record with. Sure. And, this other great bass player out there in California, Chandler.
I don't know who you're talking about.
Yeah. Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Opening and reel 2 announcement
segments.summary: Name and date are taken and reel 2 is announced at the Howard Tilton Library.

segments.title: Working with Lee Collins in LaSalle, Illinois, and the Moulin Rouge
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls leaving the Moulin Rouge in New Orleans to join Lee Collins in LaSalle, living in tiny Spring Valley because no Black residents lived nearby.

segments.title: Reel 3 and 4 openings, fish fries
segments.summary: Tape changes to reels 3 and 4; fish fries are explained as like house rent parties.

segments.title: Best and worst of the road: sleep, hotels, cheap lodging
segments.summary: Gabriel describes bus travel, segregated lodging and how he found cheap rooms and meals while others overspent.

segments.title: Clothes and washing on the road
segments.summary: He kept many shirts and washed and ironed his own clothes while other musicians travelled with a paper bag.

segments.title: Charlie Parker and the Down Beat jam session in New York
segments.summary: Parker rejoined McShann at the Down Beat, where Gabriel played bass in a jam with Ellington, Tatum, Hawkins and others, Jesse Price on drums.

segments.title: Drugs in the bands: Lamont Hamilton and the FBI
segments.summary: Gabriel kept away from drugs and tells how Lamont Hamilton, a tenor he recommended, was a drug-addled Army deserter the FBI made him help turn in.

segments.title: Jay McShann as bandleader and the band's drug use
segments.summary: He praises McShann as pianist and leader, notes that most of the band used drugs, and says McShann only drank gin.

segments.title: Recordings with McShann, Bucktown Boogie, Roy Brown sides
segments.summary: Gabriel lists records made with McShann, Witherspoon and others, his feature Bucktown Boogie, and about twenty sides with Roy Brown and with Danny Barker.

segments.title: Recording at J&M for Roy Brown: all-night party sessions
segments.summary: The Roy Brown sessions in New Orleans ran from evening to morning with drinks and sandwiches; Walter Daniels and Edgar Blanchett played.

segments.title: How records were made then: pay, takes and studio setup
segments.summary: Sessions paid $42, took full sides in one room with shared mics, unlike later isolated headphone recording.

segments.title: Roy Brown's band, 'wild kids' and R&B seriously taken
segments.summary: Gabriel did only record dates with Roy Brown, whose young sidemen such as Batman and Cat Man were unpolished, and he takes R&B seriously.

segments.title: Danny Barker sessions: Joe Parrish, Mop Mop Brown, sidemen
segments.summary: Questions about the pianist on Danny and Lou Barker dates lead to Joe Parrish, Willow Weep for Me, Mop Mop Brown and its sidemen.

segments.title: Walter Brown and the Paradise Theatre hotel bill; Blues Bailey
segments.summary: Walter Brown ran up a Detroit hotel bill and left McShann, leading to a New Orleans session and Blues Bailey's supper club job; Joe Parrish's spelling is checked.

segments.title: Jim Taylor and the New McKinney Cotton Pickers
segments.summary: Gabriel describes jazz promoter Jim Taylor, his revived McKinney Cotton Pickers, and how his own Detroit sextet outearned them.

segments.title: Reel 5 and 6 openings
segments.summary: Reel 5 starts with questions about New Orleans nightclubs, then reel 6 begins with Tad Jones gone.

segments.title: Musicians in Gabriel's Moulin Rouge group
segments.summary: He names trumpeters, clarinetists and pianists he used at the Moulin Rouge, including Little Daddy.

segments.title: Kid Ernest and the trumpeter-arranger Kill D
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls Kid Ernest Moliere and praises Kill D as a trumpeter and arranger from Robichaux's and Celestin's bands.

segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald and Peg Leg Bates with Andy Kirk
segments.summary: With Andy Kirk, Gabriel travelled with Ella Fitzgerald and one-legged tap dancer Pegleg Bates.

segments.title: Billie Holiday: the gin, singing behind the beat, tipping tricks
segments.summary: He tells how Billie Holiday threw gin at him in Detroit, her late phrasing on Lover Man, and women who picked up tips with their bodies.

segments.title: Big Apple jam sessions and playing with T. Gordon
segments.summary: Late-night jams at New York's Big Apple drew Stuff Smith, Eddie South and Harry James, and Gabriel toured army camps with a Teagarden-like trombonist.

segments.title: Playing for white strip shows and the proposed band screen
segments.summary: At the Moulin Rouge he emceed striptease shows, and a woman tried to require screens in front of Black bands.

segments.title: French Quarter bands Gabriel booked, Tony Pesina and the Johnsons
segments.summary: He was the first Black band in the French Quarter, booked bands for clubs, and started Tucker Cole and Laverne Smith.

segments.title: Pernell's piano and the Rene rhythm section
segments.summary: Gabriel discusses Alton Purnell's piano style in Rene's band and how Tisdale, Rene and he covered the rhythm.

segments.title: Joe Rene's religion and Kid Rene's character
segments.summary: Joe Rene later became religious while Kid Rene was a ladies' man; all Gabriel's family played with Kid Rene.

segments.title: Kid Rene's playing, Armstrong and the Coliseum, his records
segments.summary: Gabriel recalls Rene's range and ties to Louis Armstrong, his father managing the Coliseum Arena, and Rene's limiting records.

segments.title: Early pay stories: the quarter and the meatball
segments.summary: As a young player he got shorted $0.25 by a booker and learned to reach at the table among old-timers.

segments.title: WPA band conductors and Louis Dumaine
segments.summary: Gabriel and the interviewer sort out who led the WPA band and recall Louis Dumaine's trumpet and records.

segments.title: Brother Clarence and the dance halls, Octave on piano
segments.summary: Clarence played in Canal Street dance joints with Mike DeLay and Albert Fernandes; Octave was a good rhythm pianist.

segments.title: Sax readers, John Handy and Son Johnson
segments.summary: Gabriel discusses a reading saxophonist, John Handy's band, and Son Johnson's musicianship and sons.

segments.title: Clarence's stroke and playing in Chicago
segments.summary: Clarence quit playing after a stroke; Gabriel remembers bringing him to Chicago where he played piano in a club.

segments.title: Working in Chicago and California
segments.summary: Gabriel names Chicago clubs and says he always worked, then goes to California and San Diego after leaving McShann, recording on Capitol.
